items.title: A 1-in-300-million lottery ticket is almost always a bad investment
items.claim: Mega Millions: ~302 million possible combinations. A ticket costs $2. Jackpot of $600 million sounds like positive expected value (EV = 600M/302M = $2 — break even). But after taxes, lump sum discount, and ticket-splitting, real EV is well below $2.
items.prompt: How do you compute expected value correctly?

options.text: Sum over all outcomes of (probability * value). For a fair calculation, include ALL outcomes (not just the jackpot), tax adjustments, and the fact that big jackpots often have multiple winners who split the prize
Expected value is just the prize size

items.reveal:
Naive EV calculation for a lottery:
- Prize: $600M.
- Win probability: 1 / 302,000,000.
- EV from jackpot only: $600M / 302M ≈ $1.99.
- Ticket cost: $2.
- Naive net: -$0.01.

Real adjustments:
- Federal tax (~37% top bracket) plus state tax (variable, say 5%): take-home ~$330M instead of $600M.
- Lump sum vs annuity: lump sum is ~60% of advertised jackpot. Pre-tax lump sum: ~$360M. Post-tax: ~$200M.
- Jackpot splitting: when jackpots get large, more people play. Probability of multiple winners rises. Expected share is less than full jackpot.
- Other prizes: smaller wins (matching some numbers) contribute roughly $0.30 of EV per ticket. Better, but not enough.

Realistic EV: usually $0.50 - $1.00 per $2 ticket. Lottery is a regressive tax on the mathematically uninformed.

Linearity of expectation: E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y], even if X and Y aren't independent. A surprisingly powerful tool. The St. Petersburg paradox (already covered) is an exception where naive EV is infinite but psychological/practical value is finite.

Kelly criterion: optimal bet sizing when you have an edge. Even with positive EV, betting too much can lead to ruin. Bet fraction equals edge / odds. Most gamblers overbet, even when statistically lucky.

Applications:
- Insurance: companies sell policies with positive EV (for them); buyers accept negative EV in exchange for risk reduction.
- Investment decisions: long-run wealth is dominated by GEOMETRIC mean returns (Kelly).
- Game theory: mixed-strategy equilibria depend on equalising opponents' expected payoffs.
items.why: Expected value seems intuitive. Real computations require including hidden costs, taxes, and the structure of outcomes. The lottery survives because most players don't actually compute the math correctly — and because the entertainment value is real.

items.title: Almost every real number is transcendental — but proving it for a specific number is brutal
items.claim: Algebraic numbers (roots of polynomials with integer coefficients) are countable. The reals are uncountable. So almost every real is non-algebraic — transcendental. Yet proving that pi or e is transcendental took heroic effort.
items.prompt: How can almost all numbers have a property that's so hard to verify in specific cases?

options.text: The proofs were just very late

Cardinality arguments tell you transcendental numbers exist abundantly, but don't identify any of them; proving a specific candidate transcendental requires construction of arguments tailored to that number's algebraic relations

items.reveal:
Joseph Liouville (1844) constructed the first known transcendental: sum of 1/10 to the n factorial. The construction was explicit but artificial.

Georg Cantor (1874) showed by counting that the algebraic numbers are countable but the reals are uncountable. Therefore 'most' reals are transcendental, without identifying any.

Charles Hermite (1873) proved e is transcendental — a serious technical achievement.

Ferdinand Lindemann (1882) proved pi is transcendental. This settled the ancient problem of 'squaring the circle': constructing a square with the same area as a given circle, using only compass and straightedge, is impossible because pi is not algebraic.

The Gelfond-Schneider theorem (1934) gave a general criterion: a to the b is transcendental for algebraic a (not 0 or 1) and irrational algebraic b. So 2 to the square root of 2 is transcendental. But e + pi? No one knows. e times pi? No one knows. Even pi + e being irrational remains unproven.

Known transcendentals: e, pi, e to the pi, log 2 (natural log), specific Liouville-style constructions. Unknown: most candidate combinations.
items.why: Generic mathematical truths can be vastly easier to prove than specific instances. 'Most numbers are transcendental' is easy; 'pi is' was a century's work.

items.title: Bayesians and frequentists disagree about what probability even MEANS
items.claim: A frequentist says P(rain tomorrow) is undefined — tomorrow happens once. A Bayesian says P(rain tomorrow) = 0.3 because that's their degree of belief. Two schools, two interpretations, often the same answers in practice.

options.text: Frequentist probability is long-run frequency of repeatable events; Bayesian probability is degree of belief / credibility. The Bayesian framework can attach probabilities to one-off events (tomorrow's weather, an election outcome) that frequentists consider non-probabilistic

items.reveal:
FREQUENTIST view: probability is the long-run frequency of an event in repeated trials. P(heads) = 1/2 means: in many flips, the proportion of heads approaches 1/2.
For one-off events ('rain tomorrow', 'this defendant is guilty', 'the next president will be X'), probability is undefined.

BAYESIAN view: probability is degree of belief. P(rain tomorrow) = 0.3 means a rational degree of certainty. You can attach probabilities to anything you can think about — including one-off events.

Practical differences:
- Bayesians use prior distributions to incorporate background knowledge. Frequentists generally don't.
- Bayesians update priors with data via Bayes's theorem. Frequentists test null hypotheses (often binary accept/reject decisions).
- Frequentists ask: 'How likely is this data under H_0?' (the p-value).
- Bayesians ask: 'Given this data, what's the probability that H_0 is true?'

Most practitioners now use both depending on the problem. Frequentist tools dominate clinical trials, particle physics 'discovery thresholds' (sigma counts). Bayesian methods dominate machine learning, weather forecasting, medical diagnosis, search engines.

Historical context: frequentists dominated the 20th century. Bayesian methods were marginal until computational power (MCMC) made them practical in the 1990s. Since then, Bayesian methods have flourished.

The 'Bayesian vs frequentist' war was largely about philosophical foundations. In practice, most working statisticians now use whichever approach fits the problem best.

Edge cases: low-data or one-off events strongly favour Bayesian thinking. Repeatable experiments with lots of data give similar answers either way.
items.why: Two centuries of debate about what probability means produced two distinct philosophies, both useful for different problems. Anyone using statistics professionally needs to understand which framework they're working in.
